Synthwave

The visual side of the synthwave music microgenre of the late 2000s and 2010s, usually called the Outrun aesthetic after the 1986 Sega game Out Run: a dark night sky, a striped retrosun on the horizon, a glowing magenta laser grid that recedes to a vanishing point, chrome and airbrush-script logotypes, and 1980s sports cars and palm trees, in magenta, cyan, and violet. Wikipedia describes outrun as a term for “retro 1980s aesthetics such as VHS tracking artefacts, magenta neon, and gridlines”. Unlike vaporwave, it celebrates its sources without irony and keeps a polished, high-contrast finish.

Nostalgic / Cinematic / Energetic / Nocturnal / Retrofuturist

Visual grammar

  • Neon on night. Deep black, navy, and violet grounds carry magenta, cyan, and violet light. The sun adds yellow and orange. Colors glow rather than fill.
  • Horizon and vanishing point. A flat plane, usually a laser grid, recedes to a central vanishing point under a striped sun or a skyline. Compositions are symmetrical and centered on the horizon.
  • Chrome logotype and neon script. Heavy italic capitals rendered as chrome, with a sky-blue top, a hard horizon line, and a pink reflection below, often paired with a glowing airbrush or brush script. Secondary text is wide, spaced techno capitals.
  • Sunset, grid, car, palm. The striped retrosun, the wireframe grid, wireframe mountains, 1980s supercars such as the Testarossa, Countach, and DeLorean, palm silhouettes, and night city skylines.
  • Glow and gloss. Neon tube glows, chrome highlights, star fields, and lens flares. The finish is clean and high-definition. VHS scan lines appear as an accent, not as decay.
  • Neon outlines. Panels and buttons are dark, square boxes outlined with a thin glowing line, like a neon sign or a vector display.
  • Endless drive. The grid scrolls toward the viewer, the sun sinks, and the road runs on in loops, as in music videos and arcade attract modes.

What connects the references

The album cover is the core medium. The GUNSHIP cover has every Outrun motif in one symmetrical frame: a striped sun, a grid that changes from orange to magenta with depth, a cyan wireframe mountain, a star field, heavy brushed capitals, and a scan-line texture. Atlas reduces the scene to the striped sun on a navy starry sky. Endless Summer shows the type and surface side: a pink neon-tube script on near-black, with VHS noise and a false “©1984” as accents on a sharp image. Kavinsky’s OutRun is the photographic branch: a Testarossa, a palm, a blue night, and a red brush script, with no grid, sun, or chrome. James White made the GUNSHIP and Atlas artwork and the Blood Dragon box art.

The open images show the motif set without a product. The j4p4n banner has a striped sun, a glowing magenta mesh, and a green script word on a flat dark violet ground. The Chase The Sun still has a cyan wireframe valley that converges on a yellow sun under an indigo-to-magenta sky. Grauer’s wallpaper has the sun and grid on a violet sky, and its author calls it vaporwave. Films and games spread the look but show only parts of it. The Drive poster has the hot-pink script on a light photograph. The Kung Fury poster is a warm painted montage with a sun, lightning, palms, and a Countach. Blood Dragon has tube-lit interiors with red and cyan colour offsets and scan lines, and Hotline Miami fills whole areas with pink and magenta pixel art. The Midnight at Brixton shows the palette as stage light.

The references disagree with the record in three places. First, the grammar and rubric name chrome lettering, but no observed reference has chrome type: the title type is brush or script in GUNSHIP, OutRun, Kung Fury, Drive, Endless Summer, and the j4p4n banner. Second, the rules forbid offset shadows, but the OutRun and Kung Fury titles have blue offset shadows and the Hotline Miami scores have a dark drop shadow. Third, the rules call for a magenta grid on a black sky, but the Chase The Sun grid is cyan, and the j4p4n and Grauer grounds are violet, not black.

No website reference exists yet, so none of the CSS markers (color.gradientShare, the shadow metrics, type.centerShare, and surface.radius.median) has a measured reference, and the fingerprint stays specimen-based. The four stored images are measured for colour only, with the same lightness formula as the screenshot metric. All four are lighter than the 0.3 limit for pixels.lightness: the j4p4n banner 0.31, Grauer 0.40, Brixton 0.41, and Chase The Sun 0.54. The sun, the glowing grid, and lit haze cover much of these frames. The limit may still hold for web pages that put text on the dark part of the sky, but it does not describe the images.

Era
2006–present. Kavinsky’s “Testarossa Autodrive” (2006) and the Valerie Collective set the template, per the Aesthetics Wiki; Wikidata dates the genre to 2005. Drive (2011), Hotline Miami (2012), Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon (2013), and Kung Fury (2015) spread the look. It continues in the 2020s in games, merchandise, and music videos.

Lineage

  • Influenced by Out Run (1986 video game). Wikipedia: the term “outrun” comes from the 1986 Sega arcade racing game. PC Gamer notes that the Ferrari Testarossa and palm trees on Kavinsky’s OutRun album cover (2013) reference the game.
  • Influenced by Tron (1982 film). PC Gamer: in synthwave games “Tron’s neon lines often appear”. The glowing wireframe grid floor descends from its vector graphics.
  • Influenced by Blade Runner (1982 film). Wikipedia names Blade Runner, “both the soundtrack and the film itself”, as a key reference point. PC Gamer: “Blade Runner’s cityscapes” recur in synthwave game art.
  • Influenced by Miami Vice. Invisible Oranges, quoted by Wikipedia, describes the genre’s bright side as “Miami Vice vibes”: pastel-neon coastal nights, sports cars, and palm silhouettes.
  • Influenced by Italo disco. The Aesthetics Wiki lists Italo disco as a predecessor and compares synthwave’s airbrushed chrome script lettering to Italo disco album covers.
  • Related to Vaporwave. Wikipedia: Nicholas Diak traces both genres to the same shift toward 1980s homage after Grand Theft Auto: Vice City (2002), and calls “retrowave” an umbrella that covers both. The Aesthetics Wiki tabulates the difference: synthwave is earnest, dark, and high-contrast; vaporwave is ironic, pastel, and lo-fi.
  • Related to Darksynth. Wikidata classes darksynth as a subclass of synthwave. The Aesthetics Wiki: it swaps the neon-sunset palette for red and black, occult imagery, and horror tropes. This record covers the Outrun core, not that branch.
  • Related to Cyberpunk. The Aesthetics Wiki lists cyberpunk as a related aesthetic, and Wikipedia’s synthwave article links it. Both use neon on black; cyberpunk is dystopian and urban, synthwave nostalgic and open-horizon.

Classification rubric

The test for a new reference

Identifies the style

  • A dark night-sky ground with magenta, cyan, and violet neon light.
  • A striped sun on a horizon, a glowing perspective grid floor, or both.
  • Chrome or glowing italic lettering, often with a neon script word.
  • 1980s supercars, palm silhouettes, wireframe mountains, or night skylines, shown without irony.

Rules it out

  • A pastel or faded palette, classical statues, Windows 95 windows, or glitch decay as the main surface: that is vaporwave.
  • Rain, grime, crowded street signage, and a dystopian city mood without a horizon or a sunset: that is cyberpunk.
  • Red and black only, with occult or horror imagery: that is the darksynth branch.
  • Light or white grounds with neon used only as small accents.

Often confused with

Vaporwave
Both use a grid floor and a striped sun. Synthwave is dark, saturated, polished, and sincere, with chrome type, cars, and palms. Vaporwave is pastel, faded, glitched, and ironic, with statues, Windows 95 chrome, and fullwidth or Japanese text.
Cyberpunk
Cyberpunk is a dystopian city at street level: rain, dense signs, grime, and hacker interfaces in neon on black. Synthwave looks at an open horizon at sunset, with a clean grid, chrome logos, and nostalgia instead of dread.
Y2K aesthetic
Y2K uses silver chrome, iridescent blobs, rounded plastic, and light grounds. Synthwave chrome is a striped 1980s logotype on a black sky with neon grids, and its corners are square.
Darksynth
Darksynth is a branch of synthwave that drops the sunset palette for red, black, and horror imagery. Count it as related, not as the core.

Ideas to carry forward

  • Use a near-black navy-to-violet sky gradient as the page background, warming toward magenta at the horizon.
  • Put a striped sun on the horizon of the hero and a receding magenta laser grid below it.
  • Set display headings in heavy italic capitals with a chrome gradient: light top, hard horizon line at the middle, pink reflection below.
  • Outline panels and buttons with a 1 px neon line and a centered, blurred glow. Keep the corners square.
  • Use magenta and cyan as the two neon colors, and yellow-orange only for the sun and for figures such as prices.
  • Keep body text light on the dark part of the sky or on a dark translucent panel.

Keep the function

  • Do not use pastel or faded colors as the base. That reads as vaporwave.
  • Do not add glitch decay, Windows 95 windows, or classical statues.
  • Do not use offset or hard drop shadows. Neon glows are centered and blurred.
  • Do not put body text on the sun, the grid, or the bright horizon band.
  • Do not set long text in script or chrome type. Keep them for one or two words.
  • Do not animate the grid or flicker the neon for users who prefer reduced motion.

Useful directions: music releases, artists, and labels, retro and arcade games, club nights and festivals, esports and streaming overlays, merchandise and car culture, nostalgic campaigns.

Poor fits:

  • Finance, health, government, and other products where calm and trust come first. The style is loud and theatrical.
  • Long reading and dense documentation. Glow and dark grounds tire the eye over long text.
  • Daylight, outdoor, or nature brands. The style is nocturnal and artificial.
